title: Decomposition and abstraction
explanation: Decomposition breaks a large problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems. Abstraction removes unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters for solving the problem, e.g. a bus map shows routes but not exact road shapes.

title: Representing algorithms: flowcharts and pseudocode
explanation: Flowcharts use standard shapes (ovals for start/end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions) to show the logic of an algorithm visually. Pseudocode expresses the same logic as structured, plain-English-like text that isn't tied to any real language. Both let you plan logic before writing real code.

title: Trace tables and types of error
explanation: A trace table records the value of each variable at every step of an algorithm, so you can work out its output or spot where it goes wrong. There are three types of error: syntax errors (the code breaks the rules of the language), logic errors (the program runs but gives the wrong result) and runtime errors (the program crashes while running, e.g. dividing by zero).

title: Linear search
explanation: Linear search checks each item in a list one at a time, from the start, until it finds the target or reaches the end. It works on unsorted lists but is slow for large lists: worst case is O(n).

title: Binary search
explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves a SORTED list, comparing the middle item to the target and discarding the half that can't contain it. Much faster than linear search on large lists: O(log n).

title: Bubble sort
explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, swapping adjacent items that are in the wrong order. Each pass 'bubbles' the next-largest value into place. Simple but slow: O(n squared).

title: Merge sort
explanation: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: split the list in half repeatedly until each part has one item, then merge the parts back together in sorted order. Much faster than bubble sort on large lists: O(n log n).
code:
def merge_sort(items):
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    mid = len(items) // 2
    left = merge_sort(items[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(items[mid:])
    merged = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged

print(merge_sort([5, 1, 4, 2, 8]))  # [1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

title: Sequence, selection and iteration
explanation: The three basic building blocks of any program: sequence runs statements in order, selection (if/elif/else) chooses between branches, and iteration (for/while) repeats statements.

title: Variables, constants and data types
explanation: A variable's value can change while a program runs; a constant is fixed. Core data types: integer, real/float, Boolean, character, and string.
code:
PI = 3.14159          # constant (by convention, not enforced)
radius = 4             # variable
area = PI * radius ** 2
print(area)

title: Arithmetic, relational and logical operators
explanation: Arithmetic operators do calculations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus (the remainder), integer division and exponentiation (powers). Relational operators compare values: equal to, not equal to, less than, greater than, less than or equal to and greater than or equal to. Logical operators combine conditions: AND, OR and NOT.
code:
print(17 // 5)   # 3  (integer division)
print(17 % 5)    # 2  (modulus)
print(2 ** 8)    # 256 (exponentiation)
print(7 >= 7)    # True
print(True and not False)  # True

title: Lists and arrays (1D and 2D)
explanation: A list (array) stores an ordered collection of values, indexed from 0. A 2D list (a list of lists) stores a grid, accessed with a row and column index, which is useful for game boards or tables of data.
code:
grid = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
print(grid[1][1])  # 1

scores = [55, 72, 90]
scores.append(64)
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))

title: String handling
explanation: Strings support slicing, concatenation, and built-in methods for common tasks like finding the length, changing case, searching, splitting on a separator, and converting between strings and numbers.
code:
name = "Computer Science"
print(name.upper())
print(name.lower())
print(name[0:8])
print(len(name))
print(name.split(" "))

title: Subprograms: functions and procedures
explanation: A subprogram is a named, reusable block of code. Breaking a program into subprograms makes it easier to read, test and reuse. A function returns a value; a procedure performs an action without necessarily returning one. Parameters let you pass data in.

title: File handling
explanation: Programs can read from and write to text files to store data between runs. Using 'with open(...)' ensures the file is closed automatically even if an error occurs.
code:
with open("scores.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Alex,90\n")
    f.write("Sam,72\n")

with open("scores.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.strip().split(",")
        print(name, score)

title: Reading and writing CSV files
explanation: A CSV (comma separated values) text file stores a table of data with one row per line and the values separated by commas. Programs can write rows to a CSV file to save data and read them back later.
code:
import csv

with open("marks.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Alex", 72])
    writer.writerow(["Sam", 85])

with open("marks.csv") as f:
    for name, mark in csv.reader(f):
        print(name, mark)

title: Input validation and authentication
explanation: Validation checks that user input is sensible before it's used. Common checks are a length check, a presence check (not blank), a range check (e.g. a number between 0 and 120), a type check and a pattern check. It doesn't guarantee the data is correct, only that it's plausible. Authentication confirms who a user is, for example with an ID and password or a lookup.

title: Defensive design and error handling
explanation: Defensive design anticipates misuse: validating input (checking type, range, format), authenticating users, and handling errors gracefully so the program doesn't crash on unexpected input. Robust software copes with unexpected input and problems without failing.

title: Testing
explanation: Testing checks a program works correctly using normal data (typical valid input), boundary data (values right at the edge of what's accepted), and erroneous data (invalid input that should be rejected safely).

title: Writing readable programs
explanation: Programs are easier to read, understand and maintain when they use good layout, indentation, comments, meaningful identifiers (names that say what a variable or subprogram is for) and white space.

title: Logic gates and truth tables
explanation: AND is true only if both inputs are true. OR is true if at least one input is true. NOT inverts a single input. A truth table lists every combination of inputs and the output for each, and can have up to three inputs (8 rows). These gates combine to build up the decision logic used inside a CPU.

title: Binary numbers
explanation: Computers store all data as binary (base 2): just 0s and 1s. An 8-bit binary number can represent 256 values (0-255). Converting binary to denary: add up the place values (128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1) where there's a 1.
code:
# Convert a denary number to an 8-bit binary string
value = 156
print(format(value, "08b"))  # 10011100

# Convert binary back to denary
print(int("10011100", 2))  # 156

title: Hexadecimal
explanation: Hexadecimal (base 16) uses digits 0-9 then A-F. It's a compact way to represent binary: each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits, so it's often used for colour codes and memory addresses.
code:
value = 156
print(hex(value))       # 0x9c
print(int("9c", 16))    # 156

title: Two's complement, binary addition, shifts and overflow
explanation: Unsigned integers use every bit for the value (8 bits holds 0 to 255). Two's complement lets the same bits hold negative numbers: with 8 bits the range is -128 to +127. Binary addition follows column rules (1 + 1 = 10, carrying the 1). A logical shift moves the bits left or right, filling gaps with 0s; a left shift doubles the number and a right shift halves it. An arithmetic shift keeps the sign bit so it works on two's complement numbers. Overflow happens when the result is too big for the bits available. (Required by some boards, e.g. Edexcel.)

title: Units of data storage
explanation: Data is measured in bits and bytes (8 bits), scaling up through kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes, each roughly 1000 times the size of the previous unit.

title: Character encoding (ASCII and Unicode)
explanation: Every character a computer displays is stored as a number. ASCII uses 7-8 bits and covers basic English characters; Unicode uses more bits and can represent characters from every written language.
code:
print(ord("A"))   # 65
print(chr(65))    # A

title: Representing images
explanation: A bitmap image is stored as a grid of pixels. Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary value; more bits per pixel (colour depth) means more possible colours but a larger file size. Resolution is the number of pixels.

title: Representing sound
explanation: Analogue sound is converted to binary by sampling: measuring the amplitude (height) of the sound wave at regular intervals. The sample rate is how many samples are taken per second (in hertz), the sample interval is the time between samples, and the bit depth is how many bits are used for each sample. A higher sample rate and bit depth give better quality but a larger file.

title: Data compression
explanation: Compression reduces file size. Lossless compression (e.g. run-length encoding) removes redundancy so the original can be perfectly rebuilt. Lossy compression permanently discards some data to save more space, which is common for images, audio and video.

title: The CPU and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
explanation: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, and executes it. Main components: the Control Unit (manages the cycle), the ALU (does arithmetic and logic), the clock (keeps everything in step), registers (tiny, fast storage inside the CPU) and the bus (wires carrying data and signals between components; the address, data and control buses). Some boards also teach the von Neumann stored program concept (instructions and data held together in main memory); AQA removed this from 2027 exams, so check your board.

title: CPU performance
explanation: Clock speed (cycles per second) determines how many instructions can run per second. Cache size gives faster access to frequently used data than RAM. The number of cores lets a CPU run tasks in parallel.

title: Primary storage: RAM and ROM
explanation: RAM is volatile (fast, but cleared when powered off) and holds currently running programs and data. ROM is non-volatile and holds instructions needed to start the computer, such as the BIOS.

title: Secondary storage: solid state, magnetic and optical
explanation: Secondary storage keeps programs and data permanently, even when the power is off. Solid state storage (SSDs, USB sticks) uses electronic circuits with no moving parts: it is fast, silent and durable but costs more per gigabyte. Magnetic storage (hard disk drives) stores data as magnetised patterns on spinning platters: it is cheap and high-capacity, but slower and easier to damage. Optical storage (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) uses a laser to read a disc: it is cheap and portable but low capacity and slow. AQA no longer requires optical storage from 2027, but other boards may.

title: Embedded systems
explanation: An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to perform a specific task, e.g. a washing machine controller or a car's engine management system. Unlike a general-purpose computer, it usually runs one dedicated program and has limited memory and processing power.

title: System software and application software
explanation: System software (like the operating system) manages the computer itself: memory, processes, peripherals. Application software (like a word processor or web browser) lets the user perform specific tasks.

title: Operating systems
explanation: The operating system manages hardware resources on behalf of applications. It provides file management (organising files and folders), process management (deciding what runs when), memory management, peripheral management (via device drivers), user management (accounts, passwords and permissions) and the user interface.

title: Utility software
explanation: Utility software performs maintenance tasks that keep a system running well, e.g. anti-malware scanners, file repair, disk defragmentation, file compression, and backup tools.

title: High-level and low-level languages
explanation: High-level languages (like Python) read closer to English and are easier to write and maintain, and work on many machines, but need a translator. Low-level languages (like assembly or machine code) map closely to the hardware and run faster but are harder to write and tied to a particular processor.

title: Translators: compilers and interpreters
explanation: A compiler translates the entire program into machine code before it runs, producing a standalone executable. An interpreter translates and runs the program line by line, which is slower but easier to debug interactively.

title: Integrated Development Environments (IDEs)
explanation: An IDE bundles the tools developers need in one place: a code editor, a translator (compiler/interpreter), and a debugger for stepping through code and inspecting variable values while it runs.

title: Network types: LAN and WAN
explanation: Computers are connected in a network so they can share resources (files, printers, an internet connection) and communicate. A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area like one building and is usually owned by one organisation. A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a large area, e.g. connecting offices in different cities, and often relies on infrastructure owned by third parties such as telecoms companies.

title: Network topologies: bus, star and mesh
explanation: A topology is the way devices on a network are arranged. In a bus topology all devices share one main cable: it is cheap and simple, but a break stops the network. In a star topology every device connects to a central switch: a failed cable only affects one device, but if the switch fails the whole network goes down. In a mesh topology devices connect directly to several others: many routes mean it keeps working if a link fails, but it costs more. OCR and Edexcel require this; AQA no longer does from 2027.

title: Wired and wireless connections and network speed
explanation: Wired connections (e.g. Ethernet cables) are usually faster, more reliable and more secure. Wireless connections (e.g. Wi-Fi) are convenient and allow movement but have limited range and can suffer interference. Performance depends on speed, range, latency (the delay before data arrives) and bandwidth (how much data can be sent per second). Network speed is measured in bits per second, and transfer time = file size in bits divided by transmission rate in bits per second.

title: The internet and protocols
explanation: The internet is a global network of networks. Devices are identified by IP addresses and routers forward data between networks. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sets up communication between two devices and breaks data into packets. IP (Internet Protocol) addresses the packets and routes them across networks. HTTP is used to transfer web pages; HTTPS is the encrypted version. OCR and Edexcel also list Ethernet (wired networks), Wi-Fi (wireless networks) and FTP (file transfer); AQA no longer does from 2027.

title: Email protocols: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is used to send email from your email program to a mail server and between mail servers. IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) is used to read email from a mail server; the messages stay on the server, so you can see the same mailbox on several devices. POP3 downloads messages to your device instead. All of these operate at the application layer.

title: The 4-layer TCP/IP model
explanation: The TCP/IP model has four layers. The application layer is where network applications such as web browsers and email programs operate; the HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP and IMAP protocols operate here. The transport layer sets up communication between the two hosts and agrees settings such as the size of packets; the TCP protocol operates here. The internet layer addresses and packages data for transmission and routes the packets across the network; the IP protocol operates here. The link layer is where the network hardware, such as the network interface card (NIC), is located; operating system device drivers operate here.

title: Common cyber security threats
explanation: Malware is software designed to cause harm: viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware and key loggers. Social engineering (such as phishing) tricks people into giving up information. Brute-force attacks try many passwords automatically. Denial-of-service attacks overwhelm a service with traffic. SQL injection inserts malicious code into a database query via an input field. Hackers also exploit technical vulnerabilities such as unpatched software and out-of-date anti-malware.
code:
-- Vulnerable if a query is built like this with untrusted input:
-- "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + input + "'"
-- Safer: use a parameterised query instead
SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?;

title: Identifying and preventing vulnerabilities
explanation: Vulnerabilities can be found by penetration testing (authorised testers deliberately probe for weaknesses) and ethical hacking. Defences include firewalls (filtering network traffic), anti-malware software, access control (user accounts, passwords and access levels), physical security (locked rooms), and keeping software patched and up to date. Audit trails and code reviews also help find problems.

title: Protecting digital systems and data
explanation: Digital systems and data can be protected using anti-malware software, encryption (scrambling data so it can't be read without a key), acceptable use policies (rules on how a system may be used), and backup and recovery procedures (copies of data kept safely so it can be restored after loss or an attack).

title: Relational database concepts
explanation: A relational database organises data into tables. Each table has a primary key (uniquely identifies a row) and can be linked to other tables via a foreign key, avoiding duplicated data.

title: SQL: SELECT and WHERE
explanation: SELECT retrieves data from a table; WHERE filters which rows are returned based on a condition.

title: SQL: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
explanation: INSERT adds a new row, UPDATE changes existing rows matching a condition, and DELETE removes rows matching a condition.

title: Environmental impacts of digital devices
explanation: Digital devices affect the environment through energy consumption (running devices and data centres), manufacture (raw materials and pollution), the replacement cycle (people upgrading often) and disposal (electronic waste containing harmful materials).

title: Personal data and the law
explanation: Collecting and using personal data raises issues of privacy, ownership, consent, misuse and data protection. In the UK, the Data Protection Act and UK GDPR set rules for how personal data must be handled. The Computer Misuse Act makes unauthorised access to, or modification of, computer systems and data illegal.

title: AI, machine learning and robotics
explanation: Using artificial intelligence, machine learning and robotics raises ethical and legal questions: accountability (who is responsible when it gets something wrong?), safety, algorithmic bias (unfair results, often caused by biased training data) and legal liability.

title: Protecting intellectual property
explanation: Computer systems and software can be protected by copyright (automatically protects original work such as code), patents (protect inventions), trademarks (protect brand names and logos) and licensing (rules about how others may use the software).

title: Cultural and social impacts of technology
explanation: Technology affects different people differently. Issues include privacy and surveillance, digital exclusion (people without access to devices or the internet being left behind), and how technology changes the way people work, learn and communicate.
